newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SUBSIDIARIES POOR RESULTS KNOCK SAB SHARES.
newsitem.headline: SUBSIDIARIES POOR RESULTS KNOCK SAB SHARES.

text.p: Shares in South African Breweries Ltd (SAB) lost ground on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange (JSE) on Monday on concerns its first half results will be knocked by poor contributions from its subsidiaries.
SAB, the world's fourth largest brewer, is due to report results for the six months to September 30 on Wednesday.
By 1300 GMT shares in SAB had lost 175 cents or almost 1.5 percent to 116.75 rand, off the day's low of 116 rand.

Dealers said worse-than-expected interim earnings reports from retailer Edgars Stores , Coca-Cola bottler ABI and glass-maker Plate Glass and Shatterprufe Industries Ltd , was seen cutting into SAB's bottomline, although overall group profits were expected to improve.
"SAB is weaker on the back of poor results from Edgars and Plate Glass," one dealer said.
"There have been a lot of poor corporate reports out lately and many of them are part of the Breweries' group."
Last week Edgars posted results that showed attributable income fell five percent in the six months to end-September to 145.1 million rand.
A day later ABI said half year attributable earnings were up just one percent to 32.4 million rand and an extended capital base saw earnings per share dip two percent to 29.4 cents.
Plate Glass on Friday said first half earnings fell almost five percent to 316.4 cents a share.

Despite these negatives, analysts polled by Reuters forecast SAB group earnings rising to between 167 to 182 cents a share, with a consensus of 176 cents, up from 162.5 cents last time. Last time's dividend of 57 cents was seen rising to 60-64 cents.
Traders on Monday said the fact that JSE trading on the day was largely futures-led, with SAB heavily weighted in the basket of shares, added to the shares' woes.
"There is a lot of reverse arbitrage trading with people selling of stocks and buying futures...We have seen a lot of institutional sell orders," another trader said.

Traders said the whole equity market was blanketed in negative sentiment following central Reserve Bank governor Chris Stals' comments on exchange control abolition taking four to five years, and as the money market shortage stubbornly held above the nine billion rand level.
